lessons.title: Workplace communication
lessons.learn: Write a short professional email and soften a request.

grammar.title: could you / would you mind
grammar.explain: Indirect requests are the default at work.
grammar.pattern: Could you + verb? / Would you mind + -ing?

examples.t: Could you send the agenda by noon?
Would you mind postponing the call?
Please find the file attached.

mistakes: Don't open with 'Send me this now' to a manager.
Would you mind takes -ing, not an infinitive.

dialogue.t: Could you send feedback on the draft?
I'll follow up after lunch. The deadline is tight.
Would you mind cc'ing Maya?
Done. Agenda is attached.

lessons.title: News and current events
lessons.learn: Summarise a news story and mark what is reported, not proven.

grammar.title: reported speech (say/tell)
grammar.explain: Backshift the verb when the reporting verb is past.

examples.t: The paper said the talks had failed.
She told me the source was unnamed.
According to witnesses, nobody was hurt.

mistakes: Tell needs a person: tell me, not tell that.
Don't present a claim as a fact.

dialogue.t: Did you see the headline?
They said the talks had failed, according to one source.
The minister denied it an hour later.
Then we wait for a second source.

lessons.title: Formal versus informal register
lessons.learn: Rewrite a casual message as a formal one without changing the facts.

grammar.title: register recasting
grammar.pattern: Can you…?  →  I would be grateful if you could…

examples.t: Can you send it? → I would be grateful if you could send it.
Sorry I'm late. → Please accept my apologies for the delay.
Cheers. → Yours sincerely.

mistakes: Don't mix slang with a formal greeting.
Yours sincerely follows a named Dear X.

dialogue.t: This email says 'cheers' to a client.
Change it to 'yours sincerely' and drop the slang.
And 'can you' becomes a request.
Tone first, then send.

lessons.title: Opinions and debate
lessons.learn: Agree, disagree and concede without shutting the other person down.

grammar.title: concession then contrast
grammar.explain: Name the other view before you disagree.

examples.t: While the cost is real, the evidence is thin.
I see your point. On the other hand…
Fair enough — let's look for a compromise.

mistakes: Don't overstate a small sample as proof.

dialogue.t: I don't think the plan will work.
I see your point. The evidence is mixed.
On the other hand, waiting costs more.
Fair enough. Let's find a compromise.

lessons.title: Culture and society
lessons.learn: Describe a custom and the assumption underneath it.

grammar.title: used to vs be used to
grammar.explain: Used to + verb is a past habit. Be used to + -ing is familiarity.
grammar.pattern: used to + verb   /   be used to + -ing

examples.t: We used to remove shoes at the door.
I'm used to eating late.
She isn't used to such direct questions.

mistakes: Don't say 'I am used to go'.

dialogue.t: Is it polite to refuse a second plate?
In my family, refusing twice is fine. Don't offend the host.
I'm not used to that.
Watch the other guests.

lessons.title: Health and wellbeing
lessons.learn: Describe symptoms precisely and ask for advice without drama.

grammar.title: should / ought to / had better

examples.t: You should rest until you recover.
You'd better book an appointment today.
This medicine ought to help, but watch side effects.

mistakes: Had better is a warning, not a casual idea.

dialogue.t: How long have you had this symptom?
Three days. I'm anxious about work.
You'd better rest. I'll write a prescription.
If it continues, will you refer me?

lessons.title: Technology and change
lessons.learn: Talk about tools you rely on and what they replaced.

grammar.title: present perfect for change up to now
grammar.explain: Have/has + past participle links past change to now.

examples.t: This app has replaced our paper lists.
We haven't had an outage this month.
Have you backed up the files?

mistakes: Don't use a finished past time with present perfect.
Don't say 'I have replaced it yesterday'.

dialogue.t: The update has replaced the old menu.
Have you set a new password?
Yes. And a backup, after last week's outage.
Good. Privacy settings next.

lessons.title: Narrative and storytelling
lessons.learn: Tell a short past story with a clear time line and a point.

grammar.title: past simple vs past continuous
grammar.explain: Continuous sets the scene; simple moves the event.

examples.t: I was waiting when the call came.
Meanwhile, she was checking the map.
It turned out we had the wrong street.

mistakes: Don't use past continuous for a short completed action.
Don't pile flashbacks without time marks.

dialogue.t: So I was waiting outside when it started to rain.
Meanwhile I was on the wrong bus.
Eventually you turned up. Unexpected, but fine.
Next time I'll check the detail on the ticket.
